subtopic: MR. FANE    OFFICIAL REPORT OF DAILY PROCEEDINGS
MR. FANE    OFFICIAL REPORT OF DAILY PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege which concerns all members of this house and a good many people throughout our nation. It relates to the printing of the English version of the daily official report of the proceedings in the House of Commons.
As all our members are fully aware, this report is issued in two parts. The first part is a verbatim report of every word that is said in the House of Commons, whether in English or in French. The second part, at the back of each issue contains the English translation of the remarks made in French. Might I suggest, for the convenience of those who are not completely familiar with French, that instead of the statements made in French being printed in French in the first part, the translation of those statements be printed in English so that the whole of the first part of the daily report is in English. The original statements could then be printed in French in the second part.
In many instances questions are asked in French and answers are given in English. This necessitates, at present, looking in the back of the report in order to get the full meaning of the question and then turning back to read the answer. I note that the French version of this report is written entirely in French.

subtopic: MR. FANE    OFFICIAL REPORT OF DAILY PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for bringing this important matter to the attention of the house. Fundamentally it is really a matter of administration rather than a question of privilege. However, the subject matter has been under discussion for some time, and if it meets with his pleasure I suggest that the matter be referred for study to the committee on internal economy.

subtopic: RESEARCH INTO NUCLEAR FALL-OUT
RESEARCH INTO NUCLEAR FALL-OUT
speechtext:
1.	Is research being carried on by the Department of National Health and Welfare in respect to nuclear fall-out in Canada?
2.	How many scientists are working on this research (full time) ?
3.	Is research being carried on in respect to the protection of food supplies from nuclear fall-out?
4.	How much is being spent by the Department of National Health and Welfare on this research?
5.	Have any reports been made to the department as a result of this research?
6.	Has any action been taken based on these reports?
7.	Has the government any plans to cope with the dangerous levels of fall-out?
8.	Is there any literature available to educate citizens to cope with the dangers of fall-out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: RESEARCH INTO NUCLEAR FALL-OUT
speechtext:
1. The Department of National Health and Welfare is carrying out an extensive study of radioactive fall-out throughout Canada. The program includes systematic measurement of fall-out levels in air, precipitation and soil at a network of stations extending across Canada and into the far north. It also includes the systematic collection of milk samples from 16 localities in the populated part of Canada; these samples are assayed for iodine 131, strontium 89, strontium 90 and cesium 137. Wheat samples are collected annually from the major wheat producing areas in western Canada and analysed for strontium 90. Human bone specimens are collected at autopsy from hospitals throughout the country and assayed for strontium 90.
2.	Three chemists and one physicist are engaged full time in directing the analytical and developmental work of this program. Three other scientists are engaged part time

on various aspects of the program. Twenty highly skilled technicians are also engaged full time in this program.
3.	The department's program of measuring fall-out levels in milk and wheat represents the first step in a program designed to protect food supplies from fall-out. Milk has been selected because, for the average Canadian diet, milk and dairy products contribute more fall-out than any other single food item. Another important step in protecting food supplies involves knowing the consumption habits of Canadians of all ages. A study is currently in progress to determine the milk consumption habits of Canadians. These steps are preludes to taking actual action should it become necessary. The department, in collaboration with the Department of Agriculture and representatives of the industries concerned, has developed a plan of action for ensuring the continuing supply of acceptable milk should the levels of iodine 131 require such remedial action. Similarly the department is keeping in touch with the development of techniques for the removal of strontium 90 and cesium 137 from milk. Because of the long term nature of the build up of these elements in the body, remedial action would not need to be made effective as quickly as in the case for iodine 131. It should be emphasized that there is not now, nor has there been, need to take any of these measures.
4.	The total budget of the department's radiation protection division is $563,255 for 1963-64 and roughly half this amount relates to fall-out studies.
5.	The radiation protection division publishes a monthly report containing all the current results from the extensive fall-out studies program. These reports are available to anyone upon request and are regularly sent to all provincial departments of health and a mailing list of about 900 names. In addition, an annual report is published which presents a more detailed description of the program and its implications to health.
6.	It is not considered that the levels so far observed are such as to warrant taking any specific action. Formulation of the plan of action for dealing with high iodine 131 levels, should the need arise, was a direct outcome of the rapid rise observed in iodine 131 levels last fall.
7.	Yes, for example the plan of action for dealing with iodine 131, should the need arise. This plan will involve specific action by the dairy farmers and the dairy processors and has been made known to them. The introduction of such measures is not required at the present time.
Questions
8.	Present fall-out levels are not such as to make it desirable to take specific action to reduce the intake of fall-out. The second report of the United Nations scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiations, published in 1962, is a comprehensive technical report which evaluates the relative risk to health from various sources of irradiation and presents the most recent information on the biological effects of radiation exposure. If fall-out levels should rise to dangerous levels it is considered that more effective action could be taken by the government than by individual citizens.

1.	Does the federal government, under the terms of the Unemployment Assistance Act, pay part of the supplementary allowance authorized by the government of British Columbia to the old age security pension?
2.	If so (a) what percentage, and up to what amount is paid by the federal government (b)

what amount of liquid assets may a single person or married couple in receipt of the supplementary allowance have?
3.	Has the permissible amount of liquid assets changed recently and, if so (a) what was the previous permissible amount of liquid assets (b) what part did the federal government play in the change in the permissible amount?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	(a) The federal government, under the terms of the Unemployment Assistance Act, pays 50 per cent of assistance costs. However these exclude certain specified costs, including health costs and costs by way of mothers' allowances which are deducted on a formula basis.
No ceiling is placed by the federal government on assistance payments under the Unemployment Assistance Act. In the case of additional assistance payments to persons such as those in receipt of old age security pensions, the federal government shares in payments to the extent that they are made on the basis of a test of need which takes into consideration the applicant's requirements for food, shelter and other items, as well as his financial resources. Available information in the Department of National Health and Welfare indicates that the provincial ceiling on supplementary social allowances in British Columbia is $24. The federal government will share on the above mentioned basis in this amount or to any higher level determined by a province as necessary to meet need.
(b) The federal legislation does not set limits on the liquid assets of recipients of payments shareable under the Unemployment Assistance Act. Departmental information is that under the provincial regulations a single recipient may have liquid assets of up to $500 and a married couple may have assets of up to $1,000.
3.	(a) Information within the department is that the permissible amounts of liquid assets previously set out in provincial regulations were $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for married couples. The changes referred to were made on January 1, 1962.
(b) As a result of provincial requests for federal sharing in the cost of supplementary social allowances, discussions between federal and provincial officials were held in 1960 and
1961.	These discussions covered all phases of the program, but were primarily related to its conversion from a means test to a needs test basis. This was required to make the payments shareable under the Unemployment Assistance Act which permits sharing in additional relief payments but not in supplemental allowances or cost of living bonuses. While the limits were reduced by the province following the above discussions,

asset limits are set at the discretion of the provincial governments and vary from province to province.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the statement by Premier Khrushchev that the Soviet union is willing to sign a test ban agreement providing a non-aggression pact could be arranged between NATO and the Warsaw pact countries? Has the minister any comment to make on this statement, and what steps does the Canadian government intend to take to encourage this proposal?

subtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. The answer to the first part of the question is yes. I should say first of all, however, that the hon. gentleman's question does not make clear that it is a test ban in the atmosphere, outer space, and under water which is involved. A proposal to this effect has been put forward on several occasions by Great Britain and the United States. The indication which Premier Khrushchev has now given that he could accept such an arrangement is most welcome. It would not, however, be a substitute for a comprehensive test ban which would also call a halt to underground testing, though it would represent a significant step in that direction.
As to the second part of the question, I would say that the idea of a non-aggression pact, as I have already said in this house on May 29, could be useful in appropriate circumstances. Naturally we would have to know exactly what terms and conditions the Soviet union attaches to this suggestion, before adopting a firm decision on it or on the proposal to combine it with a partial nuclear test ban.
In mentioning the possible limitations surrounding these proposals, I do not wish to give the impression that we are underestimating their significance. A Soviet initiative looking toward some form of agreement with the

west may be of particularly great importance on the eve of the sino-Soviet meeting on July 5 and with Britain and the United States on July 15. Any proposal of this magnitude obviously requires careful study and consultation with our allies, but no effort should be spared to explore fully all the possible advantages which it may hold in terms of an east-west understanding in the broader sense.

speechtext:
Perhaps I may deal with a question asked yesterday by the hon. gentleman for Kootenay West and addressed to the Acting Prime Minister, who has referred it to me. The hon. gentleman asked whether the Canadian government was consulted by the government of the United States prior to President Kennedy's announcement in West Germany that he was willing to risk destruction of American cities in the defence of west Berlin.
In answer to that question I would say that as to the specific terms used by the President in West Germany, Canada was not consulted. However, there is of course close and continuous consultation among all NATO countries on such matters as Berlin. President Kennedy's remarks in Berlin on the indivisibility of freedom, which I take it the hon. member has in mind, were a reiteration of long standing NATO policy. They are in complete accord with article 5 of the north Atlantic treaty which states that an armed attack against one or more NATO members in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all. The remarks are also consistent with the communique on Berlin issued by the north Atlantic council in ministerial session on December 16, 1958, in which the alliance fully associated itself with the determination of the three protecting powers, the United States, Britain, and France, "to maintain their rights with respect to Berlin".
Under the circumstances there was no requirement for any special consultation in this instance.

maintopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF FAMILY ALLOWANCE COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the next few minutes, and before the question is put on the main motion, I would like to submit a grievance to the house, which I and the whole Canadian people think should be raised at this time.


When the house goes into committee of supply, opposition members traditionally avail themselves of this opportunity of raising important questions. May I tell you today that I am particularly concerned about the fact that hon. members opposite seem to have forgotten a promise made by the Liberals during the last election. I am thinking of the promise made by the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself when he stated that family allowances should be paid to children over 16 who are still going to school. I have here an official statement which the Prime Minister made in Sydney, Nova Scotia, on March 1, 1963:
(Text):
The Liberal program will extend family allowances to children beyond the age of sixteen. This is for boys and girls who remain in school.
(Translation):
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, you know that all political parties represented in this house had incorporated that item in their platform in the last election.
I have here the program of my own party and I see that, in the field of social security, the following point had been included: increase of social security. A portable pension plan, a contributory retirement plan, and old age pensions were mentioned, as were family allowances up to the age of 18 for children who were continuing their studies.
Moreover, in order to prove that there was unanimity as to the significance of such legislation, I shall quote the statements in the house of the spokesmen of the various political parties during the last session, in 1962-63.
Here are, for instance, the words of the Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition, according to page 72 of Hansard for the 1962-63 session:
Family allowances should be extended from age 16 to age 21 for all those boys and girls who are continuing their education.
There is also the following statement by the representative of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Villeneuve, on page 138 of Hansard:
-a suggestion already put forward by Social Crediters since 1945, that is to grant family allowances to all children who continue their studies until they are 21 years old.
Even the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency, who is now sitting in the house as an independent, also declared himself in favour of such a policy during the same debate, as reported on page 156.
During the last federal election, the New Democratic party took the same stand and declared itself in favour of such an extension of family allowances.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, everybody, without exception, would support such a measure; but what is being done about it today?

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but I shall take the few minutes left to refer to some remarks made by the Minister of Justice, the Acting Prime Minister.
We, on this side of the house, were glad to hear the Acting Prime Minister say that the Liberal party, the present government, promised to extend family allowances to children from 16 to 18 years of age. He was very definite in his statement. He said: "It is a pledge, you shall have it, we realize that Canadian families need additional help."
I see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) who assiduously seeks the truth, is closely following my remarks and I am sure that at the first opportunity, she will rise in the house to explain this flagrant omission on the part of the government.
Now, the Minister of Justice attempted afterwards to find excuses for his government's delay in carrying out that promise. He suggested as an excuse the fact that the order paper was already quite loaded. Well, Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard of such a paltry and senseless answer? The order paper is not a container which, once it is full, you cannot add to it. The order paper is only a list of the measures proposed to the house by the government. So, such an excuse does not stand up. Moreover, he admitted, in reply to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. H. A. Olson), that there is no administrative difficulty which could prevent them from putting that measure into force at this time, and he finally admitted that to adopt such a measure, you need funds and that the Minister of Finance has to find necessary revenues, that there is a certain priority in those matters.
Now, if that is the case, I say that it was the Liberal party's responsibility, during the last election campaign, a few months ago, to honestly tell the Canadian people: "We shall give that extended coverage of family allowances if we have the money and when we are good and ready."
But that was not the case, the Liberal party's undertaking was definite. They are untrue to their undertakings when they delay such necessary action requested by the whole Canadian people.
